rabbit.e: From Middle English rabet, rabette, from Anglo-Latin rabettus, from dialectal Old French rabotte, probably a diminutive of Middle Dutch or West Flemish robbe (“rabbit, seal”), of uncertain origin; possibly some imitative verb, maybe robben, rubben (“to rub”) is used here to allude to a characteristic of the animal.
rabbit.g: A mammal of most genera of the family Leporidae, with long ears, long hind legs and a short, fluffy tail. (Those of the larger kind are inst

rabbit.e: From Cockney rhyming slang rabbit and pork, to talk.
rabbit.g: To talk incessantly and in a childish manner; to babble annoyingly.

rabble.e: From Middle English rabel, probably from the verb (see above).
rabble.g: A bewildered or meaningless string of words.

rabble.e: From Old French roable (modern French râble), from Latin rutabulum (“a poker”).
rabble.g: An iron bar used in puddling.

race.e: From Middle English race, partially from Old English rǣs (“a race, swift or violent running, rush, onset”), from Proto-West Germanic *rās; and partially from Old Norse rás (“a running, race”); both from Proto-Germanic *rēsō (“a course”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁s- (“to flow, rush”).
race.g: A contest between people, animals, vehicles, etc. where the goal is to be the first to reach some objective.

race.e: 1560s, via Middle French race from Italian razza (early 14th century), of uncertain origin. Partially displaced native Middle English kinde (“kind, type, sort, race, nature”), whence English kind. Fully displaced native Old English cnōsl and hād.
race.g: A group of sentient beings, particularly people, distinguished by common ancestry, heritage or characteristics (see Wikipedia's article on h

radiant.e: From Middle English radyant, from Latin radiāns, radiantis, present participle of radiāre (“to emit rays or beams”).

raft.e: Late Middle English, of North Germanic origin, from West Old Norse raptr, from Proto-Germanic *raf-tra-, from Proto-Indo-European *rap-tro-, from *rep- (“stake, beam”).
raft.g: A flat-bottomed craft able to float and drift on water, used for transport or as a waterborne platform.
A large (but unspecified) number, a lot.

rafter.e: From Old English ræfter, of Germanic origin, related to the origin of raft.
rafter.g: One of a series of sloped beams that extend from the ridge or hip to the downslope perimeter or eave, designed to support the roof deck and

rag.e: From Middle English ragge, from Old English ragg (suggested by derivative raggiġ (“shaggy; bristly; ragged”)), from Old Norse rǫgg (“tuft; shagginess”), from Proto-Germanic *rawwa-, probably related to *rūhaz.

rag.g: An informal dance party featuring music played by African-American string bands.

rage.e: From Middle English rage, from Anglo-Norman rage, from Late Latin rabia, from Classical Latin rabiēs (“anger, fury”).
From Middle English ragen, from Old French rager, ragier, from the noun (see above).
rage.g: To act or speak in heightened anger.

ragged.e: From Middle English ragged, from North Germanic.
ragged.g: In tatters, having the texture broken.

raid.e: From Scots raid, from Northern Middle English rade, from Old English rād (“a riding, an expedition on horseback, road”), whence also the inherited English road (“way, street”). The earlier senses of “a riding, expedition, raid” fell into disuse in Early Modern English, but were revived in the northern form raid by Walter Scott in the early 19th century.
raid.g: A quick hostile or predatory incursion or invasion in a battle.

rail.e: From Middle English rail, rayl, *reȝel, *reȝol (found in reȝolsticke (“a ruler”)), partly from Old English regol (“a ruler, straight bar”) and partly from Old French reille; both from Latin regula (“rule, bar”), from regō (“to rule, to guide, to govern”); see regular.
rail.g: A horizontal bar extending between supports and used for support or as a barrier; a railing.

rail.e: From Middle English rail, reil, from Old English hræġl (“garment, dress, robe”).
rail.g: An item of clothing; a cloak or other garment; a dress.

railing.g: That rails; engaged in or given to violent complaining.

raiment.e: Aphetized from Middle English arayment, borrowed from Anglo-Norman arraiement and Old French areement, from areer (“to array”).

rain.e: From Middle English reyn, rein, from Old English reġn, from Proto-West Germanic *regn, from Proto-Germanic *regną, of uncertain origin. Possibly from pre-Germanic *Hréǵ-no-, from Proto-Indo-European *Hreǵ- (“to flow”), although the consonant reflexes don't match.
rain.g: Condensed water falling from a cloud.

rain.e: From Middle English reinen, from Old English reġnian, from Proto-West Germanic *regnōn, from Proto-Germanic *regnōną, from *regną (“rain”), as above.
rain.g: To have rain fall from the sky.

rainbow.e: From Middle English reynbowe, from Old English reġnboga, from Proto-West Germanic *regnabogō, from Proto-Germanic *regnabugô, from *regną (“rain”) + *bugô (“bow”). By surface analysis, rain + bow (“arch”).
rainbow.g: A multicoloured arch in the sky, produced by prismatic refraction of light within droplets of rain in the air.

rainy.e: From Middle English reyny, from Old English reġniġ, from Proto-West Germanic *regnag, from Proto-Germanic *regnagaz (“rainy”), equivalent to rain + -y.

raise.e: From Middle English reysen, raisen, reisen, from Old Norse reisa (“to raise”), from Proto-Germanic *raisijaną, *raizijaną (“to raise”), causative form of Proto-Germanic *rīsaną (“to rise”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey- (“to rise, arise”). According to Kroonen (2013), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃er- (“to stir, rise”).
raise.g: To cause to rise; to lift or elevate.

raise.e: Borrowed from Old Norse hreysi; the spelling came about under the influence of the folk etymology that derived it from the verb.
raise.g: A cairn or pile of stones.

raisin.e: From Middle English raysyn, borrowed from Anglo-Norman reysin (“grape, raisin”), from Late Latin racīmus, from Latin racēmus. Possibly a distant cognate of Persian رز (raz, “vine”).

raising.e: From Middle English reysynge; equivalent to raise + -ing.

rake.e: From Middle English rake, from Old English raca, racu, ræce (“tool with a row of pointed teeth, rake”), from Proto-Germanic *rakō, *rekô (“tool with a row of pointed teeth, rake”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to straighten, right oneself”).
rake.g: A garden tool with a row of pointed teeth fixed to a long handle, used for collecting debris, grass, etc., for flattening the ground, or for

rake.e: From Middle English rake, rakke (“pass, path, track; type of fencing thrust; pasture land (?)”), and then partly: probably from Old English racu (“bed of a stream; path; account, narrative; explanation; argument, reasoning; reason”) (compare Old English hrace, hraca, hracu (“gorge”)), from Proto-Germanic *rakō (“path, track; course, direction.
rake.g: A course, a path, especially a narrow and steep path or route up a hillside.

rally.e: From Middle French rallier (French rallier), from Old French ralier, from Latin prefix re- + ad + ligare (“to bind; to ally”).
rally.g: A public gathering or mass meeting that is not mainly a protest and is organized to inspire enthusiasm for a cause.

ram.e: From Middle English ram, rom, ramme, from Old English ramm (“ram”), from Proto-Germanic *rammaz (“ram”), possibly from *rammaz (“strong”). Possibly akin also to Danish ram (“sharp; acrid; rank”), Swedish ram (“strong; perfect”), Faroese ramur (“strong; competent”), Icelandic rammur (“strong; sturdy”).
From Middle English rammen, from the noun (see above).
ram.g: To collide with (an object), usually with the intention of damaging it or disabling its function.

ramp.e: From French rampe, from Middle French rampe, deverbal of ramper, from Old French ramper (“to crawl, climb, scale up”), from Frankish *hrampōn (“to contract oneself, wrinkle, rumple, crumple, curve”), from Proto-Germanic *hrimpaną (“to shrivel, shrink”).
ramp.g: An inclined surface that connects two levels; an incline.

rampant.e: From Middle English rampand, rampend, present participle of rampen (“to rise by climbing, shoot up, sprout, sty, ascend”), from Old French ramper (“to creep, climb”) (see below), equivalent to ramp + -and or ramp + -ant. Recorded since 1382, "standing on the hind legs" (as in heraldry), later, "fierce, ravenous" (1387).
rampant.g: Rearing on both hind legs with the forelegs extended.

rampart.e: Borrowed from Middle French rempart (“rampart of a fort”), from Old French remparer (“to defend, fortify, inclose with a rampart”), from re- (“again”) + emparer (“defend, fortify, surround, seize, take possession of”), from Old Occitan amparer, from Vulgar Latin *anteparō (“to prepare”), from ante- + parō (“to prepare”).
rampart.g: A defensive mound of earth or a wall with a broad top and usually a stone parapet; a wall-like ridge of earth, stones or debris; an embankme

random.e: From earlier randon, from Middle English randoun, raundon, from Old French randon, from randir (“to run, gallop”) (whence French randonnée (“long walk, hike”)), from Frankish *randiju (“a run, race”) or Old Norse rend (“a run, race”), both from Proto-Germanic *randijō, from *rinnaną (“run”, verb), from Proto-Indo-European *(H)r̥-nw- (“to flow, move, run”).
random.g: A roving motion; course without definite direction; lack of rule or method; chance.

rang.g: A long strip of rectangular lots of land in Quebec.

range.e: From Middle English rengen, from Old French rengier (“to range, to rank, to order”), from the noun renc, reng, ranc, rang (“a rank, row”), from Frankish *hring, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“ring, circle, curve”).
range.g: A line or series of mountains, buildings, etc.

rank.e: From Middle English rank (“strong, proud”), from Old English ranc (“proud, haughty, arrogant, insolent, forward, overbearing, showy, ostentatious, splendid, bold, valiant, noble, brave, strong, full-grown, mature”), from Proto-West Germanic *rank, from Proto-Germanic *rankaz (“straight”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“straight, direct”).
rank.g: Strong; powerful; capable of acting or being used with great effect; energetic; vigorous; headstrong.

rank.e: From Middle English rank (“line, row”), from Old French ranc, rang, reng (“line, row, rank”) (Modern French rang), from Frankish *hring (“ring”), from Proto-Germanic *hringaz (“something bent or curved”).
rank.g: A row of people or things organized in a grid pattern, often soldiers.

ransom.e: From the Middle English raunsoun, from the Old French raençon, from stem of Latin redēmptiō. Entered English ca. the 13th century.
ransom.g: Money paid for the freeing of a hostage.

rape.e: From Middle English rapen, rappen (“to abduct; ravish; seduce; rape; seize; snatch; carry off; transport”), probably from Latin rapiō (verb), possibly through or influenced by Anglo-Norman rap, rape (noun) (compare also ravish).
rape.g: The act of forcing sex upon another person without their consent or against their will; originally coitus forced by a man on a woman, but no

rape.e: From Middle English rapen, from Old Norse hrapa (“to fall, rush headlong, hurry, hasten”), from Proto-Germanic *hrapaną (“to fall down”).
rape.g: To make haste; to hasten or hurry.

rare.e: From Middle English rare, from Old French rare, rere (“rare, uncommon”), from Latin rārus (“loose, spaced apart, thin, infrequent”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“friable, thin”).

From a dialectal variant of rear, from Middle English rere, from Old English hrēr, hrēre (“not thoroughly cooked, underdone, lightly boiled”), from hrēran (“to move, shake, agitate”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōzijaną (“to stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱroHs- (“to mix, stir, cook”).
rare.g: Particularly of meat, especially beefsteak: cooked very lightly, so the meat is still red.

rase.e: From Late Middle English rasen, rasyn (“to rage; to enrage (?)”), probably from Middle Dutch râsen, râzen (“to be extremely angry, rage; to be mad, rave; to talk nonsense; of a dog: to be rabid”), from Old Dutch *rāson (modern Dutch razen).
rase.g: To be extremely angry; to rage; specifically, of a dog or wolf: to snarl in rage.

rase.e: PIE word wréh₂ds A variant of race (“(obsolete) to pluck; to pull off; to snatch; to tear”), partly influenced by raze.
rase.g: Alternative spelling of race (“to pluck or snatch (something); also, to pull (something)”).

rash.e: The Middle English word was probably influenced by the cognates listed below. The adverb is derived from Middle English rashe (“quickly, rapidly”), from rash, rasch (adjective) (see above).
rash.g: Acting too quickly without considering the consequences and risks; not careful; hasty.

rash.e: From Late Middle English rashen, rassh (“to hasten, hurry, rush”), from Old English ræscan (“to move rapidly; to flicker; to flash; to glitter; to quiver”); see further at etymology 1. probable cognates Dutch rasschen, rassen (“to hasten, hurry, rush”) (obsolete) Old Norse raska (“to dislodge, displace; to stir up”) (Swedish raska (“to hurry.
rash.g: To forcefully move or push (someone or something) in a certain direction.

rashly.g: In a rash manner; hastily or without due consideration; with precipitation.

rat.e: From Middle English raat, rat, ratt, ratte, rotte, from Old English ræt, rætt, from Proto-West Germanic *ratt, from Proto-Germanic *rattaz, *rattō (“rat”), of uncertain origin, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *Hreh₃d- (“to gnaw, scrape, scratch”).
rat.g: Any of the numerous members of several rodent families that usually have short limbs, a pointy snout, a long, hairless tail, and a body leng

rat.e: From Middle English ratten, further etymology unknown. Could be related to write.

rate.e: From Middle English rate, from Old French rate, from Medieval Latin rata, from Latin prō ratā parte (“according to a fixed part”), from ratus (“fixed”), from rērī (“think, deem, judge, estimate", originally "reckon, calculate”).

From Middle English raten (“to scold, chide”), from Old Norse hrata (“to refuse, reject, slight, find fault with”), from Proto-Germanic *hratōną (“to sway, shake”), from Proto-Indo-European *krad- (“to swing”).

rather.e: From Middle English rather, from Old English hraþor, comparative of hraþe (“soon, early, fast”). By surface analysis, rathe + -er.
rather.g: Used to specify a choice or preference; preferably, in preference to. (Now usually followed by than)

ratify.e: From Middle English ratifien, from Old French ratifier, from Medieval Latin ratifico, from Latin ratus (“reckoned”).
ratify.g: To give formal consent to; make officially valid, to sign off on.

ration.g: A portion of some limited resource, especially food, allocated to a person, group or period.

rattle.e: From Middle English ratelen, of uncertain origin; perhaps borrowed from Middle Dutch ratelen or of native origin related to Old English hratele, hrætele (“a plant known for its rustling or rattling sound”), ultimately imitative. The noun (c. 1500) is from the verb.
rattle.g: To create a rattling sound by shaking or striking.

rattle.e: From Arabic رَطْل (raṭl), variant of classical رِطْل (riṭl), ultimately from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra).
rattle.g: Alternative form of rottol: a former Middle Eastern and North African unit of dry weight usually equal to 1–5 lb (0.5–2.5 kg).

ravage.e: From French ravage (“ravage, havoc, spoil”), from ravir (“to bear away suddenly”), from Latin rapere (“to snatch, seize”), akin to Ancient Greek ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to seize”).
ravage.g: To devastate, destroy or lay waste to something.

rave.e: From Middle English raven (“to rave; talk like a madman”), from Old French raver, variant of resver, of uncertain origin.
rave.g: An enthusiastic review (such as of a play).

rave.e: From northern Middle English raven, from Old Norse ráfa (“to wander, roam”), of uncertain and obscure origin. Perhaps from a dissimilation of Proto-Germanic *wab(b)ōną (“to sway, waver, swing, shake, wobble, totter, reel, careen”), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to move, swarm, waft”).

raven.e: From Middle English raven, reven (“raven (Corvus corax); carrion crow (Corvus corone); rook (Corvus frugilegus) (?); the constellation Corvus; gall nuts of the Aleppo oak (Quercus infectoria) used to make black ink”), from Old English hræfn (“raven”), from Proto-West Germanic *hrabn (“raven”).
raven.g: Any of several, generally large, species of birds in the genus Corvus with lustrous black plumage; especially the common raven (Corvus corax

raven.e: A variant of ravin, from Middle English ravin, ravine, raven (noun).

ravening.e: Present participle of the obsolete verb raven (“to prey”).

ravenous.e: From Middle English ravenous, ravynous, from Old French ravineus. By surface analysis, ravin + -ous. As seen at raven and ravin, the word comes from a root referring to predation, not from the root referring to ravens (corvid birds).

ravine.e: Borrowed from French ravin (“a gully”), from Old French raviner (“to pillage, sweep down, cascade”), from ravine (“robbery, rapine; violent rush of water, waterfall, avalanche; impetuosity, spirit”), from Latin rapīna (cf. rapine).
ravine.g: A deep narrow valley or gorge in the earth's surface worn by running water.

ravish.e: From Middle English ravyschen, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French ravis-, present participle stem of ravir (“to seize; to take away hastily”), from Vulgar Latin *rapire, from Latin rapere.
ravish.g: To seize and carry away by violence; to snatch by force.

raw.e: From Middle English rawe, raw, rau, from Old English hrēaw (“raw, uncooked”), from Proto-West Germanic *hrau, from Proto-Germanic *hrawaz, *hrēwaz (“raw”), from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“raw meat, fresh blood”). Related also to Old English hrēow, hrēoh (“rough, fierce, wild, angry, disturbed, troubled, sad, stormy, tempestuous”).

ray.e: Via Middle English, borrowed from Old French rai, from Latin radius (“staff, stake, spoke”).
ray.g: A beam of light or radiation.

razor.e: From Middle English rasour, from Old French rasour, from raser (“to scrape, to shave”). By surface analysis, raze + -or.
razor.g: A keen-edged knife of peculiar shape, used in shaving the hair from the face or other parts of the body.

run.e: From Middle English runnen, rennen (“to run”), alteration (due to the past participle runne, runnen, yronne) of Middle English rinnen (“to run”), from Old English rinnan, iernan (“to run”) and Old Norse rinna (“to run”), both from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną (“to run”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“to boil, churn”).
